topic.timeline_arc: The Red Sea shifted from a flashpoint of the Israel‑Iran war in June 2025 to a theater of escalating Houthi attacks on commercial shipping by July, while humanitarian tragedies and rerouting of vessels amplified the region’s instability in August. By September, Houthi drones struck Israeli territory, linking the Red Sea conflict directly to the broader Israel‑Hamas war, and in October the area became a diplomatic hub for cease‑fire negotiations. The following months saw internal Sudanese violence and ambitious development projects that added new geopolitical layers, while the start of 2026 brought a series of high‑profile US‑Israel strikes on Iran, Iranian naval drills, and a US blockade that threatened to close the Red Sea to trade. By March‑April 2026 the conflict had broadened into a multi‑front war with Iran‑backed Houthi forces, alternative oil corridors, and reciprocal threats to block shipping, leaving the Red Sea poised for further escalation.
turning_points: Israel and Iran launched direct strikes that spilled into the Red Sea, marking the first major military escalation in the region.
Houthi rebels resumed aggressive attacks on commercial vessels, demonstrating a new wave of maritime insecurity.
A Houthi‑launched drone breached Israel’s air defenses and struck southern Israel, linking the Red Sea conflict to the Israel‑Hamas war.

text.summary: Coverage of Red Sea shipping runs to 36,131 articles between 2024-06 and 2026-05, of which 26,274 are high-priority stories. The direction is rising, with the last third of the window at 1.27 times the first third, and the peak month was 2026-03 with 3,536 articles. Tone is markedly more negative than ordinary news coverage, at 1.34 negative articles per positive against 0.58 for all news. The coverage is driven by the Israel-Iran war, Houthi attacks on commercial vessels and the threat of blocked waterways, which tie shipping to the wider regional conflict.
text.overview: The topic produced 36,131 articles over the window from 2024-06 to 2026-05, with 26,274 in the top priority bands covering geopolitics, disasters, regulation and major incidents. Volume peaked in 2026-03 at 3,536 articles, and the late part of the window ran at 1.27 times the early part. Negative tone stands at 1.34 per positive, against 0.58 across all news.
text.areas: The largest area of activity is People & Society › Social Sciences › Political Science with 8,147 articles, followed by Maritime Transport within Shipping & Logistics with 6,345. Law & Government › Military › Navy has 1,121 and Freight Transport has 1,096. The leading tags are 'red sea' with 27,043, 'the red sea' with 17,309, 'israel' with 11,056 and 'yemen' with 10,214, and the themes range from trade routes and freight rates to piracy prevention and naval and aerial combat operations.

Among states and regions, the Gaza Strip has 5,685 articles, Washington 3,340, Tennessee 2,493, Tehran 2,487, Capital Municipality 2,116 and Dubai 1,953.
text.people: The people most often named are Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Michael Waltz, Mohammed bin Salman, Bashar al-Assad, Lloyd Austin and Benjamin Netanyahu. Organisations include NEOM, the Rapid Support Forces, Maersk, Hapag-Lloyd, CMA CGM and the United States Fifth Fleet.
text.causes: Coverage attributes disruption to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's closing of it, a fuel cost shock and both Middle East critical waterways being closed. The impacts described are higher shipping costs, an acute crisis for the shipping industry, a severe global food price crisis, pressure on the international economy and millions being pushed back into poverty.

The freight section is much smaller at 1,042 articles, 2.88 per cent of the topic, with a late-versus-early ratio of 0.98 and 1.91 negative per positive.

text.aud0: Coverage of Red Sea shipping has become more political and diplomatic: politics stood at 21.7% and international relations at 21.3% of themed coverage in 2025. Defense held at 8.4% in 2025 after 11.2% in 2024. Recent news points to a wider regional picture, including a story on Houthi involvement possibly widening the war, one on insurers keeping ships away from the Strait of Hormuz and one on South Korea diversifying crude oil sources. The index holds 166 news articles from 2019-01-01 to 2026-06-01. The scenario figures give a central value of 37 for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, with sensitivity ranges of 25 to 49, 13 to 61 and 1 to 73 respectively, under a no-change baseline. The ranges widen each year, so the later figures carry much less certainty. Geographic evidence is thin: the only country listed for where the research is studied is China, with 2 papers.
aud0_points: Watch the share of politics and international relations in coverage, at 21.7% and 21.3% in 2025.
Track Hormuz-related insurer and supply diversification stories alongside Red Sea ones.
Treat the 2028 scenario range of 1 to 73 around a central 37 as very wide.
Note that no country-level reporting data was found, so regional exposure is not mapped.
Follow whether defense coverage, 8.4% in 2025, returns towards its 2024 level of 11.2%.
text.aud1: For the claim that Red Sea attacks increase global shipping costs, the evidence found is very thin. Only 2 papers were matched, both qualifying in stance, and both documents read were judged unrelated, so no verified verdict supports a wording recommendation. The sources are both at article tier: a 2020 study on state control of maritime transport in Sudan and a 2024 paper on Port Sudan. The related claim that shipping disruptions increase consumer prices has 2,160 papers on both poles, with 771 supporting, 514 qualifying, 25 contradicting and 850 neutral, though the 6 documents read for it were also judged unrelated. For screening, freight rates have 1 paper, on the food import bill and global shipping costs (2025), while transit time, insurance premiums, inflation and carbon emissions have 0 papers. Trade volumes show a figure of 14.1% for exports rose, but with no source paper attached.
aud1_points: Article tier: 2 papers on the Red Sea shipping cost claim, both qualifying, and both read documents judged unrelated.
Review tier: the strongest source for the consumer prices claim is a 2019 review on last-mile delivery, judged unrelated.
Gaps with no evidence found: attacks raising freight rates, attacks causing vessel rerouting, and rerouting increasing global shipping costs.
Insurance premiums, inflation and transit time have 0 papers in the screening, which means none were found, not that there is no effect.
The 14.1% trade volumes figure (exports rose) has no source or population attached.
text.aud2: The index holds 43,272 research papers from 2017 to 2025, but only 35 readable papers with real abstracts, and no the health literature index records, patents or preprints. Across the wider literature, 14,948 papers are supporting, 12,139 qualifying, 408 contradicting and 15,777 neutral, with 29.0% contested. Framing looks stable: the recent window has 27.5% cautionary across 9,818 papers against 29.8% across 11,713 earlier, a change of -2.3 percentage points, which is read as broadly unchanged. Contested share by year ran from 9.4% in 2017 to 34.6% in 2022 and 22.0% in 2025. Orientation is led by problem-identifying work (100 papers, 26.0%), and contributions are mostly empirical (207 papers). The most visible topics are ports and logistics (194) and emissions and efficiency (102), and the newest work includes a 2024 Environmental Research Letters paper on carbon emissions from the Red Sea crisis. Several listed topics, such as hermeneutics and elder care, appear unrelated to the subject.
aud2_points: Why do the three core links (freight rates, rerouting, global costs) show no evidence in the gap check?
How much of the 43,272 papers are on Red Sea shipping itself, given the off-topic themes among the leading topics?
What explains the contested share of 34.6% in 2022 compared with 12.5% in 2024?

text.triangulation: The evidence base for the claim "Red Sea attacks increase global shipping costs" consists of two documents, both classified as articles. Both documents are recorded as unrelated to the claim, and the corpus stance shows zero supporting papers, two qualifying, and zero contradicting, giving a contested_pct of 100.0, indicating active contestation. The counter‑evidence tally also records zero supports, contradictions or qualifications, and two unrelated items, and the recommendation states that no verified document verdict supports a wording recommendation. What is not shown is any direct empirical measurement linking attacks to cost increases, nor any peer‑reviewed evidence that directly supports the claim. A careful researcher should seek primary data or studies that explicitly quantify cost impacts, and verify the relevance of the two articles identified.
text.head_to_head: Comparing the two claims, the first claim ("Red Sea attacks increase global shipping costs") has zero papers on both poles and a corpus mix of zero supporting, two qualifying, zero contradicting, giving a contested_pct of 100.0, with two unrelated documents read. The second claim ("Shipping disruptions increase consumer prices") is associated with 2,160 papers on both poles, a corpus mix of 771 supporting, 514 qualifying, 25 contradicting, 850 neutral, and a contested_pct of 25.0, with six unrelated documents read. The verdict notes that the second claim has more evidence behind it. What is not shown is any assessment of the quality or relevance of the supporting papers for either claim, nor any direct linkage between Red Sea disruptions and consumer prices. A careful researcher would need to examine the substantive content of the supporting papers for the second claim and locate any comparable evidence for the first claim.
text.screening: The screening of specific risk‑factor rows returned a quantitative figure only for trade volumes, reporting a value of "14.1%" with the measure described as "exports rose". All other rows – freight rates, transit time, insurance premiums, inflation, carbon emissions – returned null values and no identified measures, though freight rates cites one paper from 2025. What is not shown is any effect size or confidence interval for freight rates or other factors, nor the population context for the trade‑volume figure. A careful researcher should locate studies that provide explicit effect estimates for the missing rows and verify the source of the 14.1% trade‑volume change.

A careful researcher would track the evolution of framing in conjunction with emerging themes to understand whether optimism or caution is gaining traction.

Apply screening to seek quantitative effect sizes for any identified factors, and consult framing and frontier analyses to understand broader narrative trends and emerging studies.
